This is highly characteristic of lumbar spinal stenosis. The absence of red flags (no bowel/bladder dysfunction, no fever, no weight loss, no night pain, no history of malignancy or infection) strongly argues against cauda equina syndrome, spinal infection (e.g., epidural abscess), metastatic disease, or inflammatory myelopathy. Plain radiographs confirm structural lumbar canal narrowing — a key morphological correlate of degenerative stenosis. While MRI is pending, the clinical-radiographic concordance is high, and degenerative lumbar spinal stenosis remains the most parsimonious, evidence-supported diagnosis. Other entities (e.g., vascular claudication, peripheral neuropathy, MS, B12 deficiency) are less likely given the symptom pattern (bilateral, posture-dependent, axial + radicular features) and lack of supporting lab/imaging evidence.

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Degenerative lumbar spinal stenosis
